article.description: Investigadores del Instituto Smithsonian revelan que la Luna se está encogiendo: detectan más de 10 mil fallas tectónicas Enséñame de Ciencia -
article.explanation:
Investigadores del Instituto Smithsonian han realizado un hallazgo significativo sobre la Luna, revelando que este satélite natural se está encogiendo. Este fenómeno ha llevado a la detección de más de 10 mil fallas tectónicas en su superficie. 

El encogimiento de la Luna se debe a procesos geológicos que han estado ocurriendo a lo largo de millones de años. A medida que el interior lunar se enfría, la corteza se contrae, lo que provoca la formación de estas fallas. Las fallas tectónicas son fracturas en la superficie donde se ha producido un desplazamiento, y su gran número indica que la Luna ha experimentado cambios significativos en su estructura.

Este descubrimiento no solo proporciona información sobre la historia geológica de la Luna, sino que también ayuda a los científicos a comprender mejor los procesos que han dado forma a otros cuerpos celestes en nuestro sistema solar. La investigación sobre estas fallas puede ofrecer pistas sobre la actividad tectónica y la evolución de la Luna a lo largo del tiempo.
article.title: Investigadores del Instituto Smithsonian revelan que la Luna se está encogiendo: detectan más de 10 mil fallas tectónicas

article.description: Terremoto de La Guaira en Venezuela fue el tercero más potente de la historia mundial: así analizaron cámaras de vigilancia para lograr el hallazgo El Tiempo
article.explanation:
Un reciente estudio ha determinado que el terremoto ocurrido en La Guaira, Venezuela, se posiciona como el tercero más potente registrado en la historia mundial. Este hallazgo se logró gracias al análisis de imágenes captadas por cámaras de vigilancia que documentaron el evento sísmico.

Los investigadores utilizaron estas grabaciones para evaluar la magnitud y el impacto del terremoto, lo que les permitió obtener datos más precisos sobre su fuerza y efectos. Este tipo de análisis es fundamental para entender mejor los fenómenos sísmicos y su comportamiento, así como para mejorar las estrategias de respuesta ante futuros eventos de esta naturaleza.
article.title: Terremoto de La Guaira en Venezuela fue el tercero más potente de la historia mundial: así analizaron cámaras de vigilancia para lograr el hallazgo

article.explanation:
**TITULAR: El Desafío Universitario de la NASA Enciende la Trayectoria de un Emprendedor de Drones**

Gavin Gardner, un joven emprendedor de Michigan, ha transformado su experiencia en el Desafío Universitario de la NASA en una exitosa carrera en el desarrollo de drones. En 2024, junto a su hermano Gryson y otros exalumnos del programa, fundó AG3 Labs, una empresa dedicada a la fabricación de drones para ejercicios de entrenamiento militar.

Gardner, quien fue estudiante de ingeniería en la Universidad Estatal de Michigan, participó en el programa de la NASA que otorga subvenciones a equipos de estudiantes universitarios. Su primer proyecto, Aerial Intra-city Delivery Electric Drones (AIDED), buscaba innovar en la entrega de carga mediante drones que se acoplaran a autobuses urbanos. Aunque el equipo decidió no comercializar esta idea debido a las estrictas regulaciones, su trabajo les valió un segundo premio en 2023 para desarrollar el sistema Laser Energized Aerial Drone System (LEADS).

La experiencia adquirida en el Desafío Universitario no solo les proporcionó habilidades técnicas, sino también conocimientos en gestión empresarial, lo que ha sido crucial para el crecimiento de AG3 Labs. Actualmente, la compañía produce miles de drones al mes, consolidándose como un actor importante en el sector de la tecnología de defensa.
article.original_title: NASA University Challenge Ignites Trajectory of Drone Entrepreneur
article.source_body: 4 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) Four co-founders of AG3 Labs –from left Matt Atkinson, Gavin Gardner, Ryan Atkinson, and Gryson Gardner – show off the military training drones their company builds at a U.S. Army event at Camp Grayling in Michigan. As a student, Gavin was on a Michigan State team twice selected for participation in NASA’s University Student Research Challenge. His NASA experience served as a foundation for the creation of AG3. AG3 Labs Five years ago, Gavin Gardner was a Michigan State University engineering student researching next-generation drone technology as part of a NASA grant. Garder expected the research to be demanding – but he was surprised that navigating the financial side of the work presented an even greater challenge. Although Gardner was used to leading fellow students in a lab setting, he and his team were completely new to things like creating budgets, handling large sums of money, and promoting their work for crowdfunding. That’s why demonstrating both engineering and entrepreneurship skills are major tentpoles of NASA’s University Student Research Challenge (USRC), an initiative that provides grants to teams of college students interested in helping the agency realize its aeronautical research goals. “Half the battle is building your product,” Gardner said recently. “The other half is selling the product in a way that everyone else can understand what you’re doing and not talking in nerdy, engineering ways.” We hope that every team that participates in the program sees, like Gavin, how they can grow technically, entrepreneurially, and use the opportunity as a launchpad for their own innovative careers. STEVEN HOLZ NASA USRC Manager Gardner and his Michigan State USRC alumni teammates are still using those lessons today, as aerospace developers. In 2024, they founded their own company, AG3 Labs, which specializes in drones for military training exercises. “I don’t think I would discredit our technical expertise in getting us to where we are today, but I know that USRC was a booster that really amplified our trajectory at such a young age,” Gardner said. NASA USRC manager Steven Holz said Gardner’s experience shows what students can accomplish when they receive both a grant and guidance – enabling a future workforce and contributing to the aviation industry. “We are proud to see the success of USRC alumni,” Holz said. “We hope that every team that participates in the program sees, like Gavin, how they can grow technically, entrepreneurially, and use the opportunity as a launchpad for their own innovative careers.” Research path Gardner’s path to running his own company began with a middle school age trip to Space Camp, where he began realizing that he wanted to be an engineer. The engineering bug also bit his brother, Gryson Gardner, and the two of them would often be found in their Michigan garage tinkering with various machinery, including drones and electronic kits. When Gardner arrived at Michigan State, he looked for extracurricular groups and found one dedicated to the increasingly popular hobby of drones. He gained hands-on, practical experience in how drones are made and operated. In 2021, Gardner received an email from a friend who told him they had just won a USRC grant from NASA for an activity called Aerial Intra-city Delivery Electric Drones (AIDED), and they needed help building a new drone. “We had this idea that instead of flying through the whole city, why can’t a drone just hitchhike a ride on a city bus like everyone else does?” Gardner said. The concept was for a cargo-carrying drone to take off, dock on top of public transportation such as a bus, charge its batteries while riding along, and then take off for its final leg of the delivery. The team built and flew a full-scale drone to prove the concept but decided against pursuing a commercial venture. “The commercial drone market kind of scared us a little bit with the large number of regulations that go into operating such a novel idea like this with flying over people in a dense city,” Gardner said. But the team’s demonstration of technical prowess and confidence led to a second USRC award from NASA in 2023 – the Laser Energized Aerial Drone System (LEADS), which focused on using a laser to transfer power directly to a drone in flight. While working on LEADS, which led to flying a prototype, Gardner’s network of contacts within the drone community expanded to include NASA personnel at the Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, who made him aware of internship opportunities, which he applied for and was accepted while in graduate school. Gavin Gardner, a University Student Research Challenge participant who went on to co-found his own drone company, also was a NASA intern in 2024 and wrote this social media post. Student challenge paves way for opportunity As his graduation in the spring of 2025 with a master’s degree approached, Gardner took the initial steps in late 2024 to co-found with his brother and other USRC alumni AG3 Labs after a friend suggested the military could use low-cost drones to test effective counter drone systems. An initial award from the U.S. Army led to more contracts, allowing the company to expand and ramp up its operations, where today their production capability enables thousands of drones to be built each month. Gardner credits his experience with USRC, especially when it came to learning more about the business side of running a technical operation, with helping create the opportunities for success he and his team are experiencing today. About the Author Jim Banke Aeronautics Senior Writer Jim Banke is a veteran aviation and aerospace communicator with more than 40 years of experience as a writer, producer, consultant, and project manager based at Cape Canaveral, Florida. He is part of NASA Aeronautics' Strategic Communications Team and is Senior Writer for the Aeronautics Division within the Research Technology Mission Directorate. In 2007 he was recognized with a Distinguished Public Service Medal, NASA's highest honor for a non-government employee. article.explanation:
**TITULAR: NASA selecciona 19 nuevas propuestas de ciencia ciudadana en 2026**

En un avance significativo para la ciencia colaborativa, la NASA ha seleccionado 19 nuevas propuestas de ciencia ciudadana en 2026, reafirmando su compromiso con la investigación accesible y participativa. Este anuncio se enmarca dentro del programa de financiamiento de semillas para la ciencia ciudadana, que busca involucrar a voluntarios en proyectos científicos innovadores.

Entre los proyectos destacados se encuentra "The Rogue Worlds Project", liderado por Jacqueline Faherty del Museo Americano de Historia Natural, que invita a los participantes a buscar planetas libres en datos de la misión SPHEREx. Otro proyecto, "Planet Hunters Roman", dirigido por Bernard Gaudi de la Universidad Estatal de Ohio, se centra en la detección de exoplanetas a través de la lente de la nueva telescopía espacial Nancy Grace Roman.

Además, el programa incluye iniciativas en heliophysics y ciencias planetarias, como "Space Weather UnderGround", que permitirá a los ciudadanos monitorear la magnetosfera terrestre mediante magnetómetros. Estas propuestas no solo amplían el alcance de la investigación científica, sino que también fomentan la participación activa de la comunidad en la exploración del cosmos.
article.original_title: NASA Selects 19 New Citizen Science Proposals in 2026
article.source_body: Explore This Section Science Citizen Science NASA Selects 19 New Citizen… Overview Resources Opportunities Citizen Science Highlights About Science Activation So far, 2026 has seen a flood of successes for volunteers who do NASA science, exemplifying NASA’s commitment to gold-standard science—transparent, reproducible and intrinsically collaborative. The Backyard Worlds: Planet 9 project announced that their project volunteers have now discovered most of the known brown dwarfs , celestial objects that are similar to planets. The Zooniverse platform, with grant from NASA, reached a milestone of 1 billion classifications. Several projects have come online that leverage new super intelligence (SI) techniques to amplify or extend the work of volunteers. More NASA volunteers are using SI to build their own data tools and help write scientific papers than ever before. Even with all of those achievements, our science community is already working on the next round of new volunteer projects and innovations. NASA’s Science Mission Directorate has selected nineteen proposals from research teams in 2026 that will result in new opportunities for you to do NASA science. The Citizen Science Seed Funding Program The Citizen Science Seed Funding Program (CSSFP-25) of NASA’s Science Mission Directorate aims to support scientists and other experts to develop citizen science projects and expand the pool of professional scientists who use citizen science techniques in their science investigations. Twelve new proposals to this program were selected. Astrophysics “The Rogue Worlds Project: Activating volunteers to uncover the hidden population of super Jupiters with SPHEREx” led by Principal Investigator Jacqueline Faherty from the American Museum of Natural History. This project will invite you to search data from NASA’s SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) mission to find free-floating planets and brown dwarfs in clusters of young stars. The SPHEREx space observatory mapping the entire sky in near-infrared wavelengths. “ Quantifying the calibrations between intrinsic galaxy merger timescales with visual pair/tidal-feature classifications” led by Principal Investigator Kameswara Bharadwaj Mantha of the University of Missouri. This project will investigate galaxy mergers, helping astronomers understand how galaxies evolve through time. You will be invited to classify realistic mock images of galaxies to help probe the statistics and dynamical evolution of galaxy mergers. “ Overlap Zoo; cosmic light tables for galaxy transparency” led by Principal Investigator Benne Holwerda of the University of Louisville. Galaxies, which glow with the light of the billions of stars they contain, also contain dust. This dust is easiest to see and quantify when it overlaps, or is backlit by, another galaxy. Help spot and characterize these rare overlapping galaxy pairs to help reveal how much dust they contain. Overlap Zoo is live! Follow this link to learn more and join the project. “ Planet Hunters Roman: Extending Citizen Science to Planetary Microlensing” led by Principal Investigator Bernard Gaudi of the Ohio State University. Exoplanets are planets orbiting stars other than our Sun. Their gravity can bend the light that travels around them. This project will invite you to spot exoplanets in data from NASA’s new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope data by the way they bend starlight. Heliophysics “Space Weather UnderGround: Deploying a low-cost Magnetometer Array with Citizens for Heliophysics Research” led by Principal Investigator Hyunju Connor at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center. Along with sunshine, our Sun produces the solar wind, an unrelenting flow of charged particles. Earth’s protective magnetic field shield deflects most of these particles, but not all, and not during extreme events. Help scientists monitor the subtle disturbances of Earth’s magnetosphere by the solar wind by setting up and monitoring your own magnetometer in Alaska. “A Citizen Science Initiative for Sonified Plasma Wave Characterization” led by Principal Investigator Lauren Blum of the University Of Colorado, Boulder. “Plasma” is the name given to the ionized gases at the edge of Earth’s magnetosphere. Solar wind, the rain of charged particles that flows out from the Sun, can interact with and generate waves in the plasma. This project will turn data from this dynamic zone into sound signals. You will be invited to listen in to identify waves in the Earth’s magnetosphere. “Revealing the Consequences of Foreshock Transients for Earth’s Magnetospheric System Through Participatory Science” led by Principal Investigator Wenli Mo at the Johns Hopkins University. This project will invite you to examine data from NASA’s MMS (Magnetospheric Multiscale) mission to identify “foreshock transients,” phenomena that have a critical but poorly understood role in space weather. The resulting dataset will help reveal how foreshock transients form, their properties, and their impacts. “IMPACT: Interactive Magnetospheric Particle Analysis and Citizen Technology” led by Principal Investigator Muhammad Fraz Bashir at the University of California, Los Angeles. Energetic particles rain down from the magnetosphere into the upper ionosphere, heating and perturbing the ionosphere, disrupting the scatter of radio waves and GPS operations. This project will invite you to help match patterns between two types of data: measurements from satellites flying overhead that detect energetic particles raining down from space and measurements from ground-based instruments that detect electromagnetic waves. By comparing these patterns, volunteers will help scientists figure out which types of space waves are causing different kinds of particle precipitation, and in turn, help scientists better understand and predict disruptions to GPS and increased radiation risks during space weather events. “Unlocking Clues About Particle Acceleration and Transport Using Particle Distributions” led by Principal Investigator Gang Kai Poh at the Catholic University Of America. NASA’s Advanced Composition Explorer, Parker Solar Probe, and Solar Orbiter are complementary missions gathering data to help scientists improve understanding of the Sun, solar wind, and space weather. Examine data from these missions to contribute to the study of the complicated flow of energetic particles from the Sun. “Data Fusion in Space: Combining Citizen Observations to Classify Solar Wind Tracers” led by Principal Investigator Cynthia Lopez-Portela of the University of Maryland, Baltimore County. This project will invite you to use their pattern-recognition skills to spot features in images of the Sun’s corona, where the solar wind begins. These features can be used as tracers to help scientists track the movement of the solar wind and build better models of how it behaves. Planetary Sciences “Mapping Lunar Iron Abundance Hotspots to Enable In-Situ Resource Utilization of Regolith Consolidation Technologies” led by Principal Investigator Karen Martirosyan at the University of Texas, Rio Grande Valley. Building a base on the Moon will require creative use of Moon materials. So what materials will future teams of astronaut base-builders have to work with? This project will invite you to help locate iron deposits in data from NASA’s Moon Mineralogy Mapper mission to help understand how the Moon formed and to aid future exploration. “Small Body Discovery and Outburst Monitoring with a Worldwide Citizen Science Telescope Network” led by Principal Investigator Ariel Graykowski at the SETI Institute. This project proposes to activate a global network of citizen scientists, each equipped with a standardized small-aperture telescope, to conduct follow-up observation of cometary outbursts and small moving bodies (comets, near-Earth asteroids, and main-belt asteroids). With their global distribution and a program of twilight observations, amateurs will complement professional surveys. The project will develop systems to automate processing of contributed images and to distribute alerts for objects of interest to the network. The Science Activation Program The Science Activation Program (SciAct) from NASA’s Science Mission Directorate supports a portfolio of competitively selected, collaborative project teams that extend the impact of NASA science. These “SciAct Teams” accomplish this by connecting people and communities – many of whom would not otherwise meaningfully engage – with NASA science data and experts, local partnerships, and authentic science experiences. Seven teams selected in the latest round of competition will engage learners with citizen science efforts directly related to NASA research priorities. Several other selected teams plan to incorporate citizen science projects or community science projects (research efforts led by and focused on specific communities) into their work. The selected proposals include: “Growing Beyond Earth: Science Activation Through Distributed Space Crop Research” led by Principal Investigator Carl Lewis at Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden, Inc. To travel or live in space, humans will need to eat. Growing Beyond Earth trains and equips middle- and high-school classrooms to conduct growth experiments with seeds and crops being evaluated for use as space food. “Sungrazer 2.0: From Armchair Discovery to Data-Driven Comet Science” led by Principal Investigator MaryKay Severino of the ARISA Lab and science lead Karl Battams of the Naval Research Laboratory. The original Sungrazer Project launched in 2006 in response to requests from citizen scientists for verification of comet discoveries. Since then, project volunteers have identified 5,204 comets and counting – the majority of known comets. Sungrazer 2.0 will bring the thrill of comet discovery to new audiences who will join the hunt for comets in images from NASA’s SOHO (Solar and Heliospheric Observatory) and STEREO (Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory) missions. “Discovering the SPARC: Space Physics through Amateur Radio Communications” led by Principal Investigator Nathaniel Frissell of the University of Scranton. Since 2017 amateur radio operators have worked together in the Ham Radio Science Citizen Investigation (HamSCI) community to study Earth’s ionosphere through carefully designed and conducted investigations of how their signals bounce off this high, ionized layer of Earth’s atmosphere. This project will bring hands-on space weather science to communities nationwide through amateur radio equipment and enroll high schools in a national research network. “Telescopes for All: Promoting audience engagement with NASA science via participatory data experiences using robotic telescopes” led by Principal Investigator Mary Dussault of the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory. This project will expand public access to a suite of 22 user-friendly, professional robotic telescopes. This access will allow people to observe, analyze, and contribute to NASA-aligned research, including the search and study of exoplanets and other citizen science projects. “Researchers Inspiring Public Participation in Lake Education and Science (RIPPLES)” led by Principal Investigator Sarah Yelton and science lead Tamlin Pavelsky, both at the University Of North Carolina, Chapel Hill. This project will collaborate with the Lake Observations by Citizen Scientists and Satellites (LOCSS) project to expand participation in lake and reservoir level monitoring. Submitted data will be used to validate observations such as those made by NASA’s SWOT (Surface Water and Ocean Topography) mission. “ARK (Antarctic Resilience and Knowledge): A Collaborative Network for Discovery and Education of Antarctica’s Iconic Species and their Changing Habitats” led by Principal Investigator Sharon Stammerjohn at the University of Colorado, Boulder. This project will invite you to examine NASA’s very high-resolution satellite images of Antarctica to study and monitor habitat changes affecting penguin, seal, and whale populations. With validation by scientists and integration of machine-assisted detection tools, this project will expand the analytical capacity of Antarctic researchers and build public literacy in polar ecosystem science. “Arctic Learning and Engagement with NASA Data for Community Solutions (Arctic LENS)” led by Principal Investigator Katie Spellman of the University of Alaska Fairbanks. This project will invite Alaskans to contribute seasonal environmental monitoring (snow, ice, aurora, spring ice-out, and green-up) in support of NASA missions including FORTE (Arctic Coastlines: Frontlines of Rapidly Transforming Ecosystems), SWOT (Surface Water and Ocean Topography), PACE (Phytoplankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem), and Landsat. Explore citizen science awards from previous years: November 2025 January 2024 September 2023 August 2022 July 2021 For more information on NASA’s citizen science programs, visit https://science.nasa.gov/citizen-science . New NASA citizen science projects launched in 2026. Top row, l-r. Galaxy Zoo: Tidal Tails, Artifact Inspector, CoCoRaHS. Middle row. Spiral Graph: Cluster Buster, Backyard Worlds: Binaries, Galaxy Zoo: Clump Scout Two. Bottom row. Overlap Zoo, Impact Flash! and Shock Detectives. article.description: Sismo en Venezuela: Estudio de la Universidad de Chile revela cómo se movió el suelo durante el terremoto en La Guaira Megatiempo
article.explanation:
Un reciente estudio realizado por la Universidad de Chile ha analizado el movimiento del suelo durante el terremoto que afectó a La Guaira, Venezuela. Este tipo de investigaciones son fundamentales para entender cómo se comporta el terreno durante eventos sísmicos, lo que puede ayudar en la preparación y mitigación de desastres en el futuro.

El estudio se centra en los patrones de movimiento del suelo, lo que permite a los científicos identificar las características específicas del sismo y su impacto en la región. Comprender estos movimientos es crucial para mejorar las construcciones y la infraestructura en áreas propensas a terremotos, así como para desarrollar mejores modelos de predicción y respuesta ante futuros eventos sísmicos. 

Este tipo de investigaciones no solo aporta al conocimiento científico, sino que también tiene implicaciones prácticas para la seguridad de las comunidades afectadas por sismos.
article.title: Sismo en Venezuela: Estudio de la Universidad de Chile revela cómo se movió el suelo durante el terremoto en La Guaira

article.description: Frente a la costa de la Isla de Vancouver, una placa oceánica se está desintegrando, brindando a los científicos su primera visión clara de una zona de subducción en proceso de muerte. Futura, el medio que explora el mundo.
article.explanation:
Frente a la costa de la Isla de Vancouver, se ha observado que una placa oceánica está en proceso de desintegración. Este fenómeno ha permitido a los científicos obtener una visión más clara de una zona de subducción que se encuentra en un estado de deterioro. Las zonas de subducción son áreas donde una placa tectónica se desliza por debajo de otra, y su estudio es crucial para entender los procesos geológicos que ocurren en el fondo marino.

La desintegración de esta placa oceánica ofrece una oportunidad única para investigar cómo estas zonas pueden cambiar con el tiempo y qué implica su "muerte" en términos geológicos. Este tipo de investigación es fundamental para ampliar nuestro conocimiento sobre la dinámica de la Tierra y los procesos que afectan la formación y destrucción de las placas tectónicas.

article.description: Estados Unidos: Blade Resources amplía en 39% estudio geofísico para identificar nuevos objetivos de cobre y oro en Arizona Revista Digital Minera REDIMIN
article.explanation:
Blade Resources ha decidido aumentar en un 39% el alcance de su estudio geofísico en Arizona, con el objetivo de identificar nuevos depósitos de cobre y oro en la región. Esta ampliación del estudio refleja el interés de la empresa en explorar más a fondo el potencial mineral de la zona, que es conocida por su riqueza en recursos naturales.

El estudio geofísico es una herramienta clave en la minería, ya que permite a las empresas obtener información sobre la composición del subsuelo sin necesidad de realizar excavaciones extensivas. Al ampliar este estudio, Blade Resources busca mejorar su comprensión de la geología local y localizar áreas que podrían ser económicamente viables para la extracción de metales preciosos.

Este movimiento se enmarca dentro de una tendencia más amplia en la industria minera, donde las empresas están invirtiendo en tecnología y estudios geofísicos para optimizar sus operaciones y maximizar la eficiencia en la búsqueda de recursos.

article.explanation:
Una información reciente del ámbito de la sismología aborda: Utilizando matemáticas tomadas de economistas, un joven de 14 años de Virginia pasó seis meses calculando dónde deberían ubicarse los sensores de terremotos. De acuerdo con la descripción disponible, Utilizando matemáticas tomadas de economistas, un joven de 14 años de Virginia pasó seis meses investigando dónde deberían ubicarse los sensores de terremotos Futura, le média qui explore le monde.

Esta publicación ofrece una síntesis preliminar de la información disponible. El contenido accesible no permite confirmar todos los detalles de la metodología, los resultados ni sus limitaciones. Los avances científicos deben interpretarse en su contexto y no como una capacidad para predecir la fecha exacta de un terremoto. Para SISMONAUTA, compartir información responsable es tan importante como conocer las nuevas investigaciones.

article.explanation: Se registró un terremoto moderado de magnitud 4.1 en el Océano Pacífico Norte, a 56 km al suroeste de Pinotepa, Oaxaca, México. El evento sísmico ocurrió el miércoles 28 de octubre de 2026 a las 14:06 hora local (GMT -7). Este tipo de actividad sísmica es común en regiones cercanas a placas tectónicas.
